title: Engineering materials
summary: Materials questions are almost always single-fact recall: a property definition, a composition percentage, a classification, or a 'which is used for' pairing. The highest-yield areas are cement (Bogue compounds, setting times, gypsum's role), bricks (classes, frog, ingredients and their effects), timber (seasoning, defects), and bitumen grades. Learn the numbers exactly — the options are usually close together.

sections.heading: Properties of building materials
sections.body:
Material properties are grouped into four families, and the examination expects you to place a named property in the right family.

- **Physical** — bulk density, density, density index, specific gravity, porosity, water absorption, water permeability, hygroscopicity, frost resistance, weathering resistance, spalling resistance, refractoriness, coefficient of softening, durability.
- **Mechanical** — strength (compressive, tensile, flexural, shear), elasticity, plasticity, hardness, toughness, brittleness, ductility, malleability, fatigue, creep, impact strength, abrasion resistance.
- **Chemical** — corrosion resistance, chemical/acid–alkali resistance, and the material's reactivity with its surroundings.
- **Thermal** — thermal conductivity, specific heat, thermal capacity, fire resistance, thermal expansion.

Four definitions that are repeatedly confused:

- **Ductility** — can be drawn out or elongated appreciably before rupture (drawn into *wire*).
- **Malleability** — can be hammered or rolled into thin *sheets* without rupture.
- **Toughness** — resists fracture under impact; absorbs energy before failing.
- **Hardness** — resists indentation, scratching and abrasion.

**Bulk density** is the mass of a material per unit of its *natural* volume, so it includes voids and pores; **density** uses the volume in the homogeneous (void-free) state. Bulk density is therefore always the smaller of the two, and the ratio between them gives the density index.

| Material | Bulk density (kg/m^{3}) |
|---|---|
| Brick | 1600 – 1800 |
| Sand | 1450 – 1650 |
| Steel | 7850 |
| Heavy concrete | 1800 – 2500 |
| Light concrete | 500 – 1800 |
| Granite | 2500 – 2700 |

**Porosity** is the ratio of the volume of pores to the total volume of the material. It governs thermal conductivity, strength, bulk density and durability — a more porous material is weaker, lighter and a better insulator.

sections.heading: Stones
sections.body:
Rocks are classified three ways, and the examination usually asks for the classification *basis*.

- **Geological** — igneous (granite, basalt, trap), sedimentary (sandstone, limestone, shale), metamorphic (marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, slate from shale, gneiss from granite).
- **Physical** — stratified (sandstone, limestone, slate), unstratified (granite, trap, basalt), foliated (slate).
- **Chemical** — siliceous (silica dominant: granite, quartzite, sandstone), argillaceous (clay dominant: slate, laterite), calcareous (calcium carbonate dominant: limestone, marble).

The metamorphic parent–product pairs are examined almost every sitting, so learn them as pairs. **Quartzite is siliceous** and is the metamorphic form of sandstone.

Requirements of a good building stone: crushing strength above about 100 N/mm^{2} for heavy work, water absorption under 0.6% by weight, specific gravity above 2.7 for heavy engineering, hardness coefficient above 14 for road work, fine and even grain, freedom from cracks and cavities, and good weathering resistance. The **crushing strength test** on stone uses a 40 mm cube saturated for 72 hours.

sections.heading: Bricks
sections.body:
**Constituents of good brick earth and what each does** — this mapping is a favourite question.

| Ingredient | Typical % | Function / effect of excess |
|---|---|---|
| Silica (SiO_{2}) | 50 – 60 | Prevents shrinking, cracking and warping; gives uniform shape. Excess makes the brick brittle. |
| Alumina (Al_{2}O_{3}) | 20 – 30 | Gives plasticity for moulding. Excess causes shrinkage and warping on drying. |
| Lime (CaO) | ≤ 5 | Binds particles, prevents shrinkage; fuses sand. Excess melts the brick and it loses shape. |
| Iron oxide (Fe_{2}O_{3}) | 5 – 6 | Gives the **red colour**; improves impermeability and strength. Excess gives a dark blue/blackish colour. |
| Magnesia (MgO) | < 1 | Gives a yellow tint and reduces shrinkage. Excess causes decay. |

The **presence of sand (silica) in brick earth prevents warping, shrinking and cracking**. Iron oxide is what imparts the red colour.

Harmful ingredients: lime in *lumps* (slakes, expands and splits the brick), pebbles and gravel (prevent uniform mixing, weaken the brick), alkalis or reh (cause efflorescence — white patches), iron pyrites (oxidise and disintegrate the brick), organic matter (leaves pores, makes bricks porous and weak).

The **frog** is the indentation on the face of a moulded brick. It keys the mortar and holds the manufacturer's mark; it is provided in hand-moulded and pressed bricks and is laid **facing upward** so it fills with mortar. A frog is not provided on bricks used in flooring or as a wire-cut brick.

**Compressive strength (IS 1077) — first class brick ≥ 10.5 N/mm^{2}, second class ≥ 7.0 N/mm^{2}, third class ≥ 3.5 N/mm^{2}, and the minimum for common burnt clay brick is 3.5 N/mm^{2}.**

**Water absorption after 24 hours immersion — first class brick not more than 20% by weight (not more than 15% for class designation above 12.5, and not more than 22% for second class).** Beware of collections that quote this as "0.15": that is a mis-typed 15%.

Brick manufacturing stages, in order: preparation of clay (unsoiling, digging, cleaning, weathering, blending, tempering) → moulding → drying → burning. **Burning is what develops the strength** and hardness; drying only removes moisture so the brick does not crack when burnt. Clamp burning is cheap and suits small quantities; kiln burning (Bull's trench, Hoffman's) is continuous and gives more uniform quality.

**Bloating** is the swelling of a brick caused by gases trapped in the clay — the defect is also called swelling. **Efflorescence** is the white salt deposit from alkalis. **Lamination** is thin laminae from air trapped during moulding.

sections.heading: Cement
sections.body:
**Bogue compounds** and what each controls is the single most examined item in this subchapter.

| Compound | Symbol | Typical % | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tricalcium silicate | C_{3}S | ~40 – 50 | **Early strength** (first 7 days); hardens rapidly; high heat of hydration |
| Dicalcium silicate | C_{2}S | ~25 – 30 | **Ultimate / later strength**; hydrates slowly; low heat |
| Tricalcium aluminate | C_{3}A | ~8 – 12 | **Flash set**; highest heat of hydration; weakest against sulphate attack |
| Tetracalcium aluminoferrite | C_{4}AF | ~6 – 10 | Poor cementing value; gives colour |

So: **early strength is due to C_{3}S**; **ultimate strength is due to C_{2}S**; **the highest heat of hydration is from C_{3}A**.

**Gypsum (CaSO_{4}·2H_{2}O), added at about 3 – 5%, retards the setting of cement — it increases the setting time** by reacting with C_{3}A and preventing a flash set. This is the most common single-fact cement question.

**Raw materials** — limestone is the primary raw material (supplying CaO, ~60–65%), with clay/shale supplying silica and alumina. The main hydration product responsible for strength is **C-S-H gel (calcium silicate hydrate)**, with calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)_{2}) liberated as a by-product.

**Setting time (IS 4031) for ordinary Portland cement — initial setting time not less than 30 minutes; final setting time not more than 600 minutes (10 hours).** For rapid hardening cement the initial set is also 30 minutes; for low-heat cement it is 60 minutes.

**Storage.** Cement loses strength on storage because it absorbs moisture from the air (air-set). Roughly 20% strength loss in 3 months, 30% in 6 months and 40% in 12 months. So **the strength of cement decreases after storage**.

**Types and their use** — OPC (general), rapid hardening (early formwork removal, cold weather), low heat (mass concrete, dams), sulphate resisting (foundations in sulphate soils), Portland pozzolana (mass concrete, marine works, more durable and less permeable), blast furnace slag (mass concrete, low heat), **white cement (painting, flooring, decorative and architectural finishes)**, coloured cement (decorative).

sections.heading: Lime
sections.body:
Lime is classified by the clay content of the parent limestone, which is what decides whether it sets in water.

- **Fat lime** (quicklime, high calcium lime) — from limestone with less than about 5% clay; slakes vigorously, expands 2–2.5 times, sets **only in air** by absorbing CO_{2} (carbonation). Used for whitewashing, plastering and mortar in ordinary masonry.
- **Hydraulic lime** — contains 5–30% clay; **sets under water** as well as in air. This is the lime used in **lime mortar** for masonry, and is the answer when a question asks which lime is used in lime mortar.
- **Poor lime** — more than 30% clay; slakes slowly, sets poorly, gives weak mortar.

Hydraulic lime is sub-graded as feebly hydraulic (5–10% clay), moderately hydraulic (11–20%) and eminently hydraulic (21–30%).

**Slaking** is the addition of water to quicklime (CaO) to make hydrated lime (Ca(OH)_{2}), an exothermic reaction. IS classes: Class A (eminently hydraulic, for structural work), Class B (semi-hydraulic, masonry mortar), Class C (fat lime, finishing), Class D (dolomitic, whitewashing), Class E (kankar lime), Class F (siliceous dolomitic, plastering).

**Plaster of Paris is obtained by calcining gypsum** — heating gypsum to about 120–160 °C drives off part of the water of crystallisation. It sets very rapidly (5–10 minutes), so retarders are added for practical use.

sections.heading: Timber
sections.body:
**Seasoning is the removal of moisture (sap) from felled timber** to a level in equilibrium with the surroundings, so the timber is dimensionally stable, resists decay and takes preservatives and paint. It does **not** add strength directly — it makes the timber usable — although dry timber is stronger than green timber.

Methods:

- **Natural (air) seasoning** — stacked in a shed; slow (2–4 years) but reliable.
- **Kiln seasoning** — controlled hot air; fast and thorough but costlier and can weaken timber if rushed.
- **Water seasoning** — sap replaced by water, then dried; quick but reduces elasticity and durability.
- **Boiling** — quick, but expensive and reduces elasticity.
- **Chemical (salt) seasoning** — soaked in a salt solution, then dried.
- **Electrical seasoning** — high-frequency current heats the timber; very quick but very costly, and **its drawback is that it causes splitting** and can reduce strength.

Defects due to conversion: chip mark, torn grain, diagonal grain, wane. Defects due to natural forces: knots, shakes (heart, cup, ring, star), twisted fibres, upsets, rind galls, burls. Defects due to fungi: dry rot, wet rot, blue stain, brown rot, sap stain, heart rot.

**Fibreboard density (IS 3348)** — hardboard/high-density above 800 kg/m^{3}, **medium density 350–800 kg/m^{3}**, low density (insulation board) below 350 kg/m^{3}. Note that some circulating collections quote "600 to 800" or "960" for medium density; the standard band is 350–800 kg/m^{3}, with 960 kg/m^{3} being firmly in the hardboard range.

sections.heading: Metals and alloys
sections.body:
**Metallurgy is the science and process of extracting metals from their ores** and preparing them for use.

Ore-dressing sequence, in order: **crushing and grinding → concentration (dressing) → calcination/roasting → smelting → refining.**

- **Concentration of ore** is the removal of gangue (impurities) from the ore.
- **Washing** is the operation that removes the clay adhering to iron ore — a water jet carries the lighter clay away. Some circulating keys wrongly give "pressing" here; pressing is a forming operation, not an ore-dressing one.
- **Calcination** heats the ore below its melting point in the absence (or limited supply) of air to drive off moisture and CO_{2}; **roasting** does it in an excess of air to remove sulphur.

**Carbon content** — wrought iron below 0.25% (about 0.05–0.25%), **steel 0.25% up to about 1.5%** (mild steel 0.15–0.30%, medium 0.3–0.6%, high carbon 0.6–1.5%), cast iron 2–4%. Increasing carbon increases hardness, brittleness and strength, and reduces ductility and weldability.

**Stainless steel — the main alloying element is chromium** (about 12–18%, which forms the passive chromium-oxide film), usually with nickel. Other pairings worth memorising: manganese steel for wear resistance, nickel steel for toughness, and **steel is the preferred formwork material where the formwork is to be reused repeatedly**, because of its rigidity, smooth finish and very high number of reuses.

sections.heading: Paints and varnishes
sections.body:
Constituents of oil paint and their functions:

| Constituent | Function |
|---|---|
| **Base** (white lead, red lead, zinc oxide, titanium oxide) | Body of the paint; gives opacity and durability |
| **Vehicle / binder** (linseed oil) | Carries the base; binds the film and gives it adhesion |
| **Pigment** | **Imparts the colour** and improves hardness |
| Solvent / thinner (turpentine) | Makes the paint workable; evaporates |
| Drier | Accelerates drying by oxygen absorption |
| Extender / filler | Reduces cost, increases volume |

So **the constituent that gives paint its colour is the pigment**, and **red lead is the pigment used for corrosion resistance** on structural steel (a red-lead primer is the classic anti-corrosive first coat).

**Varnish** is a transparent or nearly transparent solution of resin in oil, turpentine or alcohol. **Lacquer is a spirit varnish** — resin (shellac) dissolved in alcohol/spirit; it dries very quickly by evaporation. Oil varnish is durable and suited to exterior work; spirit varnish is not.

sections.heading: Asphalt, bitumen and tar
sections.body:
- **Bitumen** — a petroleum residue, soluble in carbon disulphide; the binder used in road works.
- **Tar** — obtained by the destructive distillation of coal or wood; contains free carbon, is more temperature-susceptible and less durable than bitumen.
- **Asphalt** — a mixture of bitumen with inert mineral matter (natural asphalt, or mastic asphalt for flooring and waterproofing).

**Cutback bitumen** is bitumen thinned with a volatile solvent for cold application — RC (rapid curing, with naphtha/petrol), MC (medium curing, with kerosene), SC (slow curing, with diesel). **Bitumen emulsion** disperses bitumen in water with an emulsifier, used for cold-weather work, patch repair and tack coats.

**Blown / oxidised bitumen** is air-blown at high temperature; it is stiff and rubbery and is used for roofing, pipe coating and joint filling. **Plastic bitumen** — bitumen with a thinner and a filler — is used for **filling cracks** in masonry and for stopping leaks; the closely related use for sealing cracks in an asphalt pavement is **crack filling / crack sealing**.

Bitumen tests and what each measures: penetration test (grade/consistency, in units of 0.1 mm), ductility test (elongation before break, minimum 50 cm for paving grades), softening point (ring-and-ball, temperature at which it flows), viscosity, flash and fire point (safe heating temperature), specific gravity, and the solubility/loss-on-heating tests for purity.

formulas.label: Bulk density
formulas.expression: ρ_{bulk} = M / V_{natural}   (includes voids and pores)
formulas.note: Always less than the true density, which uses the void-free volume.

formulas.label: Porosity
formulas.note: Higher porosity means lower strength, lower bulk density and better insulation.

formulas.label: Water absorption of brick
formulas.note: 24 h immersion. First class brick: not more than 20% by weight.

formulas.label: Coefficient of softening
formulas.expression: K = strength when saturated / strength when dry
formulas.note: A measure of how much a material weakens when wet.

formulas.label: Density index
formulas.note: Indicates the degree to which the volume is filled with solid matter.
